question: Barb the baker creates a new temperature system for baking bread, Breadus, which is linearly based on Fahrenheit. Bread rises at \(110\text{ F}^{\circ},\) which is \(0\) on the Breadus scale. Bread bakes at \(350\text{ F}^{\circ},\) which is \(100\) on the Breadus scale. Bread is done when its internal temperature is \(200\text{ F}^{\circ}.\) What is this temperature on the Breadus scale?
solution:
A linear temperature conversion makes corresponding temperature increases proportional. We can therefore compare how far \(200^\circ\mathrm{F}\) lies between the two given temperatures.

The Fahrenheit interval from rising to baking is
\[
350-110=240,
\]
while the increase from rising to being done is
\[
200-110=90.
\]
Thus \(200^\circ\mathrm{F}\) is
\[
\frac{90}{240}=\frac38
\]
of the way from \(110^\circ\mathrm{F}\) to \(350^\circ\mathrm{F}\). Its Breadus reading is the same fraction of the way from \(0\) to \(100\):
\[
0+\frac38(100-0)=37.5.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{37.5}\) on the Breadus scale, choice \(\text{D}\).
